newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - U.S., UK look a firmer bet than stocks. [corrected 15:38 gmt]
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - U.S., UK look a firmer bet than stocks. [corrected 15:38 gmt]

text.p: U.S. and UK bond markets look better value than stocks in the current climate of expected interest rate rises, but equity markets in Europe and Japan have investor appeal, analysts said on Friday.
"Markets will be looking to how things pan out in 1998, to see if the tightening process is going to be lengthy," said Stephen Hannah, chief economist at IBJ International here.
U.S. and other bond markets are already pricing in a quarter point rise in U.S. interest rates after the next Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on March 25, analysts said.
The federal funds target rate currently stands at 5.25 (corrects from 5) percent.
The U.S. 30-year bond is proving resilient, and pulled back to end the day higher on Thursday after crossing the seven percent yield threshold on comments by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan.
Greenspan said that ideally the Fed must act pre-emptively to fight inflation. His remarks were interpreted as a signal of imminent higher interest rates.
European bonds and stocks also opened higher on Friday.
Longer term, bond markets are responding well to the threat of higher U.S. interest rates and the effect on yield value, analysts said.
But equity markets have failed to take on board the full impact of possible rate rises on corporate profits, they added.
"I prefer bond markets -- equity markets have yet to discount potential tightening moves for the rest of the year," said Kirit Shah, chief strategist at Sanwa International in London.

The gap between annualised two-year T-note yields of around 6.40 percent and U.S. dividend yields of under two percent is well above the strategic three point difference, and presents a buying opportunity in debt markets, Shah said.
"There are strong signals from investors that they regard (long bond) seven percent yields as quite attractive," said Hannah.

British bonds and stocks mirror the U.S. situation most closely, analysts said, because of the widely held view that the incoming British government will rapidly raise interest rates after the election on May 1.
Recent British economic data add to the picture of a buoyant economy which will need to be held in check, they added.
But elsewhere in Europe and in Japan, equity markets have "There is still surplus capacity," said Hannah.
"Corporate profits can still expand without running into specific problems from policy tightening."

David Brown, chief European economist at Bear Stearns International in London, said European equity markets had been slow to catch on to the downturn in bonds caused by market talk of a delay to European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), particularly in peripheral markets such as Italy.
If there is a delay, "that is going to have a knock-on effect on the equity markets," said Brown.
But short-term equity losses could be substituted by longer term gains, he added.
"Any sell-off in equities should be a buying opportunity, as a delay in EMU will lessen the austerity crisis affecting European economies and provide growth opportunities."
